questions.q: Phase I metabolism of most drugs converts the active drug into:
questions.exp: The Phase I flowchart reads: most drugs (active) → drug broken down → inactivated, generating a functional group. (Book p11)

questions.q: In Phase I metabolism, a prodrug (inactive) is:
opts: Inactivated by conjugation with glucuronic acid
Broken down to a functional group and activated
Converted into a more lipid-soluble compound
questions.exp: The Phase I flowchart shows 'Pro drug (inactive) → drug broken down → Activated', with a functional group generated — this is how prodrugs are switched on. (Book p11)

questions.q: The product of Phase I metabolism, common to both prodrug activation and drug inactivation, is:
opts: Drug conjugated to a -ve charged moiety
questions.exp: Both arms of the Phase I flowchart converge on 'Drug + Functional group', which is then handed over to Phase II for conjugation. (Book p11)

questions.q: Phase II metabolism consists of:
opts: Conjugation of the drug with a functional group
Oxidation of the drug by CYP450
Hydrolysis of the drug by esterases
Reduction of the drug by microsomal enzymes
questions.exp: The heading reads 'Phase II: Drug + Functional group', with an arrow labelled 'conjugate (-ve charged)' showing that Phase II attaches a conjugate to the Phase I product. (Book p11)

questions.q: The conjugate added in Phase II metabolism carries which charge?
opts: Variable charge depending on the drug
questions.exp: The Phase II diagram labels the conjugate '(-ve charged)'; this charged conjugate is what makes the metabolite water soluble. (Book p11)

questions.q: Conjugation in Phase II renders the drug:
opts: Ionised and water soluble, easily excreted
Volatile and excreted by the lungs
questions.exp: Phase II output: drug + functional group + conjugate → ionized and water soluble → easily excreted. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the two phases of drug metabolism?
opts: Phase I conjugates; Phase II oxidises
Phase I generates a functional group; Phase II conjugates it
Both phases are performed only by gut bacteria
questions.exp: Phase I reactions create a functional group on the drug (oxidation being the most common), and Phase II then conjugates that group, making the drug ionised, water soluble and easily excreted. (Book p11)

questions.q: The note about placebo states that placebo:
opts: Contains a subtherapeutic dose of drug
questions.exp: Note: placebo does not contain any drug — it is used purely for the psychological (expectation) effect in trials. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which antimalarial drug is listed as a prodrug?
questions.exp: The prodrug list begins with proguanil — an inactive compound activated by metabolism into its antimalarial form. (Book p11)

questions.q: Regarding ACE inhibitors as prodrugs, the book states:
opts: Ramipril and other ACE inhibitors are prodrugs, except captopril and lisinopril
Only captopril and lisinopril are prodrugs
No ACE inhibitor is a prodrug
questions.exp: 'Ramipril & other ACE inhibitors (except Captopril, Lisinopril)' — captopril and lisinopril are already active, so they are the two exceptions to the prodrug rule. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which pair of drugs from the prodrug list is used for Parkinson's disease or its related movement disorders?
questions.exp: The list includes 'Dipivefrine, Levodopa' — levodopa is the classic prodrug converted to dopamine in the brain. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which antisecretory (antidiarrhoeal) drug is listed as a prodrug?
questions.exp: Racecadotril appears in the prodrug list; it is hydrolysed to its active enkephalinase-inhibiting metabolite. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which two anticancer drugs are listed as prodrugs?
questions.exp: The list ends with 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine — both require intracellular metabolic activation to their cytotoxic nucleotides. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which of the following pairs from the prodrug list are both used in acid-related disorders (ulcer disease)?
questions.exp: The third prodrug line lists 'Oxcarbazepine, Omeprazole'; omeprazole is activated in acid-secreting gastric parietal cells, and oxcarbazepine is reduced to its active metabolite. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a prodrug as listed in the book?
questions.exp: Lisinopril (along with captopril) is specifically named as the exception — it is not a prodrug, unlike ramipril and the other ACE inhibitors. (Book p11)

questions.q: A 60-year-old man on ramipril for hypertension has poor blood-pressure control. The reason ramipril needs metabolic activation is that it is a:
opts: Prodrug requiring conversion to its active form
Drug with a very short half-life
Competitive inhibitor of its own metabolism
questions.exp: Ramipril is a prodrug (ramipril is converted to the active ramiprilat); prodrugs are inactive as given and must be metabolised before they act. (Book p11)

questions.q: The mnemonic for Phase I reactions is:
questions.exp: ORCHAD stands for Oxidation, Reduction, Cyclization, Hydrolysis, Aliphatic hydroxylation, Aromatic hydroxylation and Deamination — the Phase I reactions. HIPS Dance, LUNJA and WIPE belong to other topics. (Book p11)

questions.q: The most common (m/c) Phase I reaction is:
questions.exp: The list marks 'Oxidation (m/c)' — oxidation, catalysed chiefly by the CYP450 enzymes, is the commonest Phase I reaction. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which of the following belongs to the Phase I reaction list?
questions.exp: Hydrolysis is one of the ORCHAD Phase I reactions; sulfation, glucuronidation and methylation are Phase II conjugation reactions. (Book p11)

questions.q: Aliphatic hydroxylation and aromatic hydroxylation are classified as:
questions.exp: Both appear in the ORCHAD Phase I list (A = aliphatic hydroxylation, A = aromatic hydroxylation) and are carried out by microsomal CYP450 enzymes. (Book p11)

questions.q: Phase I reactions are carried out by:
questions.exp: 'Phase I reactions are enabled by microsomal CYP450 enzymes' — the cytochrome P450 system is the principal Phase I machinery. (Book p11)

questions.q: Phase II reactions are named after:
opts: The organ in which they occur
The Phase I reaction that preceded them
questions.exp: The heading states 'Phase II Reaction: Named after the conjugate' — e.g. glucuronidation is named after glucuronic acid added as the conjugate. (Book p11)

questions.q: The most common (m/c) Phase II reaction, and the only microsomal one, is:
questions.exp: 'Glucuronidation (m/c): microsomal' — glucuronidation is the commonest Phase II reaction and the exception that takes place in the microsomes. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which group of Phase II reactions are non-microsomal?
opts: Glycination, glutathionation, acetylation, methylation and sulfation
questions.exp: The brace labelled 'Non microsomal reactions' brackets glycination, glutathionation, acetylation, methylation and sulfation — glucuronidation is left outside because it is microsomal. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which Phase II reaction is listed as microsomal?
questions.exp: Glucuronidation is annotated 'microsomal', while acetylation, glutathionation, glycination, methylation and sulfation are grouped as non-microsomal. (Book p11)

questions.q: CY (cytochrome) is best described as a:
opts: Heme protein that binds oxygen and facilitates metabolism
Conjugate added in Phase II metabolism
Pump that effluxes drugs from cells
Plasma protein that binds acidic drugs
questions.exp: 'CY (cytochrome): Heme protein that binds oxygen → facilitates metabolism' — the haem iron is what allows CYP450 to oxidise drugs. (Book p12)

questions.q: The '450' in cytochrome P450 refers to:
opts: Enzymes discovered in plant pigment, absorbing light of 450 nm wavelength
The molecular weight of the enzyme in kilodaltons
The number of substrate families known
questions.exp: 'P450: enzymes discovered in plant pigment, absorbs light of 450 nm wavelength' — the name comes from the spectral absorption peak of the reduced CO-bound pigment. (Book p12)

questions.q: In the nomenclature CYP1A2, the numeral '1' denotes the:
questions.exp: '1 → denotes the family. A → subfamily. 2 → geneisoform number' — so CYP1A2 = family 1, subfamily A, isoform 2. (Book p12)

questions.q: In the nomenclature CYP1A2, the letter 'A' denotes the:
questions.exp: The letter is the subfamily (A in CYP1A2); the first number is the family and the last number the geneisoform. (Book p12)

questions.q: CYP1A2 is the example given in the book to illustrate which aspect of CYP nomenclature?
opts: The microsomal location of CYP enzymes
The induction of CYP by rifampicin
questions.exp: Eg CYP1A2 is used to explain that the numeral denotes family, the letter the subfamily and the final numeral the geneisoform number. (Book p12)

questions.q: Which drugs are metabolised by CYP1A2?
questions.exp: CYP1A2: paracetamol, tacrine and theophylline. (Book p12)

questions.q: Which two drugs are metabolised by CYP2B6?
questions.exp: CYP2B6: 6-mercaptopurine and methyldopa. (Book p12)

questions.q: CYP2C9 metabolises which two drugs?
questions.exp: CYP2C9: phenytoin and warfarin — the basis of the classic warfarin-phenytoin interaction. (Book p12)

questions.q: CYP2C19 performs which two opposite functions on its substrates?
opts: It metabolises omeprazole and activates clopidogrel
It metabolises clopidogrel and activates omeprazole
It activates both omeprazole and clopidogrel
It metabolises both omeprazole and clopidogrel
questions.exp: CYP2C19 metabolises omeprazole but activates clopidogrel — one enzyme, opposite clinical consequences for its two substrates. (Book p12)

questions.q: In the CYP2C19 note, omeprazole and clopidogrel are described as:
opts: Competitive inhibitors (substrates of the same enzyme)
Two drugs metabolised by different enzymes
questions.exp: They are bracketed as 'Competitive inhibitors (substrates of the same enzyme)' — both compete for CYP2C19. (Book p12)

questions.q: A patient on clopidogrel after stenting is prescribed omeprazole for dyspepsia. The expected consequence is:
opts: Omeprazole decreases the effect of clopidogrel
Omeprazole increases the effect of clopidogrel
No interaction, as they act on different enzymes
Omeprazole increases clopidogrel levels causing bleeding
questions.exp: As stated: 'Omeprazole decreases the effect of clopidogrel' — it competes with clopidogrel for CYP2C19, so less clopidogrel is activated to its active metabolite. (Book p12)

questions.q: CYP2D6 metabolises which group of drugs?
opts: Psychiatric drugs (antidepressants, antipsychotics), opioids and β-blockers
questions.exp: CYP2D6 metabolizes psychiatric drugs (antidepressants, antipsychotics), opioids and β-blockers. (Book p12)

questions.q: Besides metabolising drugs, CYP2D6 is stated to activate:
questions.exp: Under CYP2D6: 'Activates: Tamoxifen' — CYP2D6 converts tamoxifen into its active metabolite endoxifen. (Book p12)

questions.q: Chronic consumption of ethanol leads to:
questions.exp: The flowchart reads: ethanol — chronic consumption → CYP2E1 upregulation. (Book p12)

questions.q: Following chronic ethanol consumption, paracetamol is metabolised to increased amounts of NAPQI, resulting in:
questions.exp: Chronic ethanol → CYP2E1 upregulation → paracetamol → ↑NAPQI → hepatotoxicity; CYP2E1-generated NAPQI is the toxic metabolite of paracetamol. (Book p12)

questions.q: Paracetamol is metabolised predominantly by which enzyme, as noted in the flowchart?
questions.exp: '(Paracetamol metabolised by CYP2E1 >> CYP1A2)' — CYP2E1 accounts for the greater part, which is why alcohol-induced CYP2E1 upregulation predisposes to paracetamol hepatotoxicity. (Book p12)

questions.q: An alcoholic with chronic liver disease takes an overdose of paracetamol. The risk of hepatotoxicity is high because:
opts: CYP2E1 is upregulated, generating more NAPQI
CYP2E1 is inhibited, so paracetamol accumulates unchanged
Renal excretion of paracetamol is enhanced
questions.exp: Chronic alcohol upregulates CYP2E1, shifting more paracetamol to the toxic NAPQI pathway and causing hepatotoxicity. (Book p12)

questions.q: The most common (m/c) CYP450 enzyme is:
questions.exp: 'CYP3A4 (m/c): metabolises >50% of drugs' — it is the most common isoform, handling more than half of all drugs. (Book p12)

questions.q: CYP3A4 metabolises:
questions.exp: CYP3A4 metabolises >50% of drugs, and mifepristone is the example given. (Book p12)

questions.q: The example of a drug metabolised by CYP3A4 given in the book is:
questions.exp: 'metabolises >50% of drugs (eg: mifepristone)' — mifepristone is quoted as a CYP3A4 substrate. (Book p12)

questions.q: Atazanavir causes which adverse effect through glucuronidation-related metabolism?
questions.exp: Under glucuronidation: 'Atazanavir (antiviral) — Cause → Steven Johnson syndrome'. (Book p13)

questions.q: Irinotecan, an anticancer drug, causes:
questions.exp: Under glucuronidation: irinotecan (anticancer) → toxicity (its glucuronidation by UGT determines the severity of diarrhoea and neutropenia). (Book p13)

questions.q: Atazanavir and irinotecan are both contraindicated in:
questions.exp: The brace states 'Both drugs are c/i in Crigler Najjar syndrome' — glucuronidation is already defective there, so these glucuronidated drugs are contraindicated. (Book p13)

questions.q: Estrogen is metabolised in the liver by:
opts: Phase I with CYP3A4, then Phase II glucuronidation
Phase I with CYP2D6, then sulfation
questions.exp: In the flowchart, liver metabolism of estrogen = Phase I with CYP3A4 and Phase II glucuronidation, forming estrogen + glucuronic acid. (Book p13)

questions.q: The liver converts estrogen into:
opts: Estrogen + glucuronic acid, which is water soluble
Estrogen + sulfate, which is lipid soluble
Free estrogen, which is water soluble
Estrogen + glutathione, which is lipid soluble
questions.exp: Phase II glucuronidation yields 'estrogen + glucuronic acid (water soluble)', which is then excreted in bile into the small intestine. (Book p13)

questions.q: In the small intestine, estrogen glucuronide undergoes:
opts: Active transport into the portal vein
questions.exp: Small intestine: glucuronidase action by gut bacteria splits the conjugate, releasing 'estrogen broken down + lipid soluble'. (Book p13)

questions.q: After gut bacterial glucuronidase acts on estrogen glucuronide, the estrogen becomes:
questions.exp: The deconjugated 'estrogen broken down + lipid soluble' is reabsorbed (returning to the liver along the arrow) — the basis of enterohepatic circulation. (Book p13)

questions.q: Enterohepatic circulation of estrogen is described as producing:
questions.exp: The boxed label reads 'Enterohepatic Circulation: Extension of normal T½' — recycling through gut and liver keeps estrogen in the body longer. (Book p13)

questions.q: Antibiotics interfere with estrogen recycling by:
opts: Killing gut bacteria, reducing enterohepatic circulation of estrogen
questions.exp: The flowchart shows antibiotics (with a 'kill' symbol) → ↓enterohepatic circulation of estrogen — by removing the gut bacteria that deconjugate it. (Book p13)

questions.q: The clinical consequence of antibiotics reducing enterohepatic circulation of estrogen is:
questions.exp: Antibiotics → ↓enterohepatic circulation → ↓T½ → OCP failure; the estrogen is cleared faster and contraceptive cover is lost. (Book p13)

questions.q: A woman on oral contraceptive pills develops diarrhoea and is given antibiotics. Loss of contraceptive efficacy occurs because:
opts: Gut bacteria are reduced, so estrogen is not deconjugated and recycled
The antibiotic induces CYP3A4 and destroys estrogen
The antibiotic binds estrogen in plasma
The antibiotic increases renal excretion of estrogen
questions.exp: Antibiotics lower gut bacteria and thus reduce enterohepatic circulation of estrogen, shortening its T½ and causing OCP failure. (Book p13)

questions.q: The mnemonic for the drugs undergoing acetylation is:
questions.exp: HIPS Dance = Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide and Dapsone — the acetylation substrates. (Book p13)

questions.q: Which of the following drugs undergo acetylation?
opts: Hydralazine, isoniazid, procainamide, sulfonamide and dapsone
questions.exp: The HIPS Dance list: Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide, Dapsone. (Book p13)

questions.q: Which important adverse effect is bracketed against the acetylated drugs?
questions.exp: The brace against the HIPS list reads 'Can cause drug induced SLE' — hydralazine and procainamide are the classic culprits. (Book p13)

questions.q: A patient on hydralazine for hypertension develops arthralgia, rash and a positive ANA. The likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Hydralazine belongs to the acetylated HIPS drugs (Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide, Dapsone) which can cause drug induced SLE. (Book p13)

questions.q: Drug interactions in this chapter occur due to:
opts: Changes in plasma protein binding only
Competition for renal tubular secretion only
questions.exp: 'D/t microsomal enzymes induction or inhibition' — the drug interaction table is built entirely around CYP450 microsomal induction and inhibition. (Book p14)

questions.q: Enzyme inducers act by:
opts: ↑ enzyme → ↑ metabolism → ↓ plasma concentration → drug failure
questions.exp: Inducers increase enzyme amount, so metabolism increases, plasma concentration falls and the drug fails to act. (Book p14)

questions.q: Enzyme inhibitors act by:
opts: ↓ enzyme → ↓ metabolism → ↑ plasma concentration → drug toxicity
↑ enzyme → ↑ metabolism → ↓ plasma concentration → drug failure
questions.exp: Inhibitors reduce the enzyme, metabolism falls, plasma concentration rises and the drug becomes toxic. (Book p14)

questions.q: Which group lists the enzyme inducers from the table?
opts: Griseofulvin, rifampicin, chronic alcohol, benzopyrene, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and St. John's wort
Quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin and valproate
questions.exp: Examples of inducers: griseofulvin, rifampicin, alcohol (chronic), benzopyrene, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and St. John's wort. (Book p14)

questions.q: St. John's wort is described in the table as:
opts: A plant used to treat depression, and an enzyme inducer
A herbal diuretic with no interactions
An enzyme inducer used for epilepsy
questions.exp: 'St. John's wart (Plant used to treat depression)' is listed among the inducers — a herbal antidepressant that induces microsomal enzymes and can cause contraceptive failure. (Book p14)

questions.q: Benzopyrene, an enzyme inducer in the table, is best known as:
questions.exp: Benzopyrene, a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon of tobacco smoke, is listed among enzyme inducers (as it induces CYP1A1/1A2). (Book p14)

questions.q: Which of the following are listed as enzyme inhibitors?
opts: Acute alcohol consumption, quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole, valproate, erythromycin/clarithromycin, grapefruit juice and diethylcarbamazine
Griseofulvin, rifampicin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and St. John's wort
questions.exp: The inhibitor column lists acute alcohol consumption, quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole, valproate, erythromycin/clarithromycin, grapefruit juice and diethylcarbamazine. (Book p14)

questions.q: Alcohol appears in the table as both inducer and inhibitor. The correct distinction is:
opts: Acute consumption inhibits; chronic consumption induces
Acute consumption induces; chronic consumption inhibits
Both acute and chronic consumption inhibit
Alcohol is not an enzyme inducer
questions.exp: The table lists 'Alcohol (Chronic)' among inducers and 'Acute alcohol consumption' among inhibitors — the classic acute-inhibition, chronic-induction pattern. (Book p14)

questions.q: Grapefruit juice is included in the table because it is:
questions.exp: Grapefruit juice appears in the inhibitor list — it inhibits CYP3A4 in the gut wall, raising levels of co-administered CYP3A4 substrates. (Book p14)

questions.q: Diethylcarbamazine, listed as an enzyme inhibitor, is clinically used as:
questions.exp: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the antifilarial agent listed among enzyme inhibitors. (Book p14)

questions.q: Which of the following is an enzyme inducer?
questions.exp: Rifampicin is a classic microsomal enzyme inducer; cimetidine, ketoconazole and valproate are enzyme inhibitors. (Book p14)

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT an enzyme inhibitor?
questions.exp: Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer; cimetidine, ciprofloxacin and ketoconazole are all listed inhibitors. (Book p14)

questions.q: In the interaction table, the effect of an inducer on metabolism and plasma concentration respectively is:
questions.exp: For inducers the cascade is ↑enzyme → ↑metabolism → ↓plasma concentration → drug failure. (Book p14)

questions.q: Which statement about microsomal enzyme interactions is TRUE?
opts: Inducers cause drug failure, while inhibitors cause drug toxicity
Inducers cause toxicity, while inhibitors cause failure
Both inducers and inhibitors cause failure
questions.exp: The summary of the table: inducers increase metabolism and lower plasma concentration, leading to drug failure; inhibitors reduce metabolism and raise plasma concentration, leading to toxicity. (Book p14)

questions.q: In the case of OCP failure due to rifampicin, the clinical significance column advises:
opts: Change the method of contraception (IUD or condoms), or avoid enzyme inducers, or ↑ the dose of drugs
Stop rifampicin immediately in all patients
Double the OCP dose and continue rifampicin
Add an enzyme inhibitor to the regimen
questions.exp: For OCP failure due to rifampicin the actions given are: change the method of contraception (IUD or condoms), or avoid enzyme inducers, or ↑ the dose of drugs (eg phenytoin & retigabine). (Book p14)

questions.q: Which examples are given for increasing the dose of a drug when an enzyme inducer cannot be avoided?
questions.exp: The table cites '(Eg. Phenytoin & Retigabine)' as drugs whose dose is increased when an inducer has to be continued. (Book p14)

questions.q: Erythromycin, an enzyme inhibitor, leads to theophylline toxicity causing:
questions.exp: Clinical significance of inhibitors: 1. Erythromycin → theophylline toxicity (↓ arrhythmia, ↓ fibrillation) — the arrows indicate the toxic manifestations. (Book p14)

questions.q: Clarithromycin, an enzyme inhibitor, can precipitate:
questions.exp: '2. Clarithromycin → Statin toxicity' — by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism of statins, clarithromycin can cause myopathy/rhabdomyolysis. (Book p14)

questions.q: A patient on theophylline develops arrhythmia after being started on erythromycin. The mechanism is:
opts: Reduced renal tubular secretion of theophylline
questions.exp: Erythromycin inhibits the microsomal enzyme metabolising theophylline, so theophylline levels rise and arrhythmia/fibrillation result. (Book p14)

questions.q: A patient on simvastatin develops muscle pain and raised CK after a course of clarithromycin. This is because clarithromycin:
opts: Inhibits statin metabolism, causing statin toxicity
Induces statin metabolism, causing statin failure
questions.exp: Clarithromycin is a microsomal enzyme inhibitor → statin toxicity; less statin is metabolised, so levels rise and myopathy occurs. (Book p14)

units.title: Phase I and Phase II Metabolism: Two Steps to Excretion
units.guide: Phase I breaks the drug down to yield a functional group, activating a prodrug or inactivating an active drug; Phase II then conjugates that group with a negatively charged moiety, making the drug ionized, water soluble and easily excreted. Placebo, by contrast, contains no drug at all.

units.title: Prodrugs: The Full List
units.guide: Prodrugs are inactive as given and require metabolism for activation: proguanil, ramipril and other ACE inhibitors (except captopril and lisinopril), oxcarbazepine, omeprazole, dipivefrine, levodopa, racecadotril, 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine. Knowing the exceptions and the drug classes is what makes this list clinically usable.

units.title: Phase I Reactions (ORCHAD) and Phase II Conjugations
units.sec: Reactions of drugs in the phases · p11
units.guide: Phase I reactions follow ORCHAD — Oxidation (m/c), Reduction, Cyclization, Hydrolysis, Aliphatic and Aromatic hydroxylation, Deamination — all enabled by microsomal CYP450 enzymes. Phase II reactions are named after the conjugate added; glucuronidation is the most common and the only microsomal one, while glycination, glutathionation, acetylation, methylation and sulfation are non-microsomal.

units.title: CYP450 Nomenclature and the Enzyme Group
units.guide: Cytochrome is a haem protein that binds oxygen and facilitates metabolism; the 450 refers to the 450 nm light absorbed by these enzymes first found in plant pigment. In CYP1A2 the number denotes the family, the letter the subfamily and the final number the geneisoform.

units.title: Substrate Map of the CYP Isoforms
units.sec: Drugs metabolised in phase I (by CYP450 types) · p12
units.guide: CYP1A2 handles paracetamol, tacrine and theophylline; CYP2B6 handles 6-mercaptopurine and methyldopa; CYP2C9 handles phenytoin and warfarin. CYP2C19 metabolises omeprazole but activates clopidogrel, and the two compete, so omeprazole decreases the effect of clopidogrel; CYP2D6 metabolises psychiatric drugs, opioids and β-blockers and activates tamoxifen.

units.title: Ethanol, Paracetamol and the CYP3A4 Rule
units.guide: Chronic ethanol consumption upregulates CYP2E1, which metabolises paracetamol far more than CYP1A2 does, so more NAPQI is generated and hepatotoxicity follows. CYP3A4 is the most common isoform, metabolising more than 50% of drugs — mifepristone being the quoted example.

units.title: Glucuronidation and Crigler Najjar Syndrome
units.sec: Drugs metabolised in phase II: Glucuronidation · p13
units.guide: Glucuronidation handles atazanavir, which can cause Steven Johnson syndrome, and irinotecan, which causes toxicity. Because the pathway itself is deficient in Crigler Najjar syndrome, both drugs are contraindicated in that condition.

units.title: Estrogen, Enterohepatic Circulation and OCP Failure
units.guide: Estrogen is metabolised in the liver by Phase I (CYP3A4) and Phase II glucuronidation to a water-soluble conjugate that enters the small intestine. There gut bacterial glucuronidase releases lipid-soluble estrogen, which is reabsorbed — enterohepatic circulation extending its normal T½. Antibiotics kill these bacteria, shorten the T½ and cause OCP failure.

units.title: Acetylation and Drug-Induced SLE (HIPS Dance)
units.guide: Acetylation substrates follow the mnemonic HIPS Dance — Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide and Dapsone — and all of them can cause drug induced SLE, often with arthralgia, rash and a positive ANA.

units.title: Enzyme Inducers vs Inhibitors: The Interaction Table
units.guide: Inducers raise enzyme amount, increase metabolism and lower plasma concentration producing drug failure; inhibitors do the reverse and produce toxicity. Inducers: griseofulvin, rifampicin, chronic alcohol, benzopyrene, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, St. John's wort. Inhibitors: acute alcohol, quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole, valproate, erythromycin/clarithromycin, grapefruit juice, diethylcarbamazine.

units.title: Clinical Significance: OCP Failure, Theophylline and Statin Toxicity
units.guide: When rifampicin causes OCP failure the options are to change the contraceptive method (IUD or condoms), avoid enzyme inducers, or increase the dose of the interacting drug as with phenytoin and retigabine. Inhibitor toxicity is shown by erythromycin causing theophylline toxicity with arrhythmia and fibrillation, and clarithromycin causing statin toxicity.
